This post reached the top 3 on Hacker News this week, with 400+ comments.

If you ship AI-written PR descriptions or design docs, **your reviewers are probably thinking the same thing.**

panel.big: I don't want to read what you didn't write

slides.text:
The author, engineer Colin Breck, keeps seeing the same pattern: someone builds a feature with AI, then **has the AI write the design doc after the fact.**

He calls the result unreadable: pages of detail, no explanation of why.

He cites a survey of developers: if they suspect AI wrote a blog post, **78% stop reading** and 71% avoid that author afterward.

A reviewer can't stop reading your PR. My guess is they keep going and trust you a little less.

panel.small: stop reading when it sounds like AI

slides.text:
His explanation for why these docs are so hard to read: **the person who prompted the AI already has the context.** They wrote the prompts and saw the code.

The reviewer gets "changed X, split Y, added tests for Z" and has to guess what matters.

What I want from a PR description is short: **why the change exists, how risky it is, and where you want me to look.**

I'd take a rough paragraph in your own words over a page of generated summary.

He isn't against AI. On a recent paper he used it to check his sentences against the source code and fill in citations.

**He still wrote every line himself.** The only part the AI wrote was the abstract.

My rule for anything a teammate has to read: **I write it, and AI checks it against the code.**

The model can catch a typo or a wrong column name. It has no idea why I made the change, and that's the part my reviewer needs.

What's the worst AI-generated PR or design doc you've had to review?

**Tell me in the comments,** and save this for the next time you write one.
